content: If inclusion in tuberculosis services is not feasible, efforts should be made to improve the recording and reporting of tuberculosis data by sex and age. Tuberculosis and HIV programs should encourage the use of case-based electronic recording and reporting systems, as well as mobile phones and other e-health communication tools. When a child is diagnosed with tuberculosis (TB), they should also be tested for HIV if their HIV status is unknown. In many settings, a diagnosis of TB or HIV can lead to stigma and discrimination, which can significantly impact the family unit, adding to the burden of caring for children with TB or TB/HIV during illness and death. A family-centered care model, which focuses on the continuum of care for the entire family rather than the individual, is essential. This approach requires a multidisciplinary strategy to address all the family’s needs. Key principles of this continuum of care include: Integrating care with prevention to provide a comprehensive and holistic system for managing TB and TB/HIV. Offering non-discriminatory and non-judgmental care and prevention. Maintaining confidentiality and respecting basic rights. Providing clinical and nursing care, as well as home-based care, to alleviate TB and HIV symptoms and prevent opportunistic infections. Offering counseling and psychosocial support services. Mobilizing community resources for cost-effective, comprehensive, and holistic care. Educating, supervising, and supporting staff and volunteers. When a child is identified as the “index” case of TB or HIV, it is common to find other family members with TB who may also require further assessment. Parents and siblings of children with TB or TB/HIV should be assessed for TB and HIV. Healthcare workers must evaluate the extent of care that family members can provide and identify what additional support is needed from external sources. This requires understanding: The family’s knowledge of TB. Whether the family has acknowledged the child’s TB (and HIV) diagnosis. The parents’ health and psychological condition. The parents’ ability to provide physical care for the child. The individuals who can support the family, their age, and health status. Whether these individuals are willing and able to assist in caring for the child. The social services available to the family in their community. Practical support for families with a child diagnosed with TB should include: Psychological support for family members receiving the child’s test results, allowing time for questions about the diagnosis and management. Assistance in helping the family understand the child’s TB through appropriate information and educational materials, including details about treatment, its frequency and duration, available health services, and the family’s role in ongoing care. Addressing specific issues for older children and adolescents with TB or TB/HIV. Referring other family members, especially siblings and close contacts, for TB screening. Providing isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) and referring for cotrimoxazole preventive therapy (CPT) and antiretroviral therapy (ART) as indicated. Counseling on the nutritional needs of infants, young children, and other affected family members. Ensuring health facilities arrange appointments with identified services and community resources before the family leaves the facility. Community support is vital in managing TB in children. While specialized care at healthcare facilities has been the traditional approach, not all TB cases require hospital-based investigations and care. Decentralized care delivered at the community level, integrated with family and child services, offers several advantages: All family members needing TB care can receive it simultaneously and in the same location. Time and money are saved when care is provided closer to home. Continuity of care is maintained between the patient’s home, community, and local health center. Community support is enhanced, potentially improving treatment adherence and addressing barriers to long-term care, such as transportation costs and loss of wages during illness and clinic visits. Involving local schools is also important. Educating teachers and staff about the needs of children with TB/HIV, the necessity of frequent clinic visits, and the importance of regular medication can help reduce stigma in schools. For children who cannot attend school, faith-based organizations and other strong community groups can play a role in supporting children with TB and their families.
